title: Your Course Is Their Cosmos
author: Mark Bauerlein
summary: Mark Bauerlein argues that a syllabus does far more than assemble readings: in any course with a historical or aesthetic dimension it quietly hands students a picture of reality. He recalls his 11th-grade American fiction class in 1975, where an aloof teacher spent the first week reading aloud a long list of canonical American novels, pausing over each, before narrowing to the year's syllabus. Far from feeling burdened, the 16-year-old Bauerlein found the list reassuring: it revealed a lineage and a tradition, made each assigned novel feel important, and made reading a 'noble and fateful endeavor.' He saw the same pattern in a UCLA graduate theory course that began with Plato and Aristotle before reaching contemporary schools. His move is to generalize from these experiences to a claim about what students infer from course design: a coherent canon teaches that human events have significance and achievement awaits discovery. He contrasts this with the depthless, unstructured flood of media that shapes today's teenagers and may feed rising anxiety, urging teachers to ask what their syllabi imply about the universe.
points: Bauerlein's teacher's first-week roll call of great American novels established the syllabus as a slice of an exclusive tradition rather than personal taste.
Knowing that superior works existed and were ranked gave an uncertain 16-year-old a trustworthy map and heightened his investment in each assigned novel.
Whether intended or not, a course's syllabus answers implicit questions about whether history has meaning, human nature is good, and life is significant.
A chronological canon teaches that there is significance in human events, while a jumbled mix of pop culture and classics might teach the opposite.
Against a media environment of depthless, random stimuli, a coherent humanities course can counter young people's anxiety by offering a world worth joining.
quotes: I accepted the authority of the teacher’s roll call without thinking. I liked it. To know that there was a set of superior creations, and that I would read some of them was an assurance. I was 16, curious but uncertain, and here was a ranking of things I could trust.

He took his time, no rushing through the items, as if each figure and book deserved a pause. As the list grew, a bigger picture began to form, not one thing followed by another, but a lineage with each writer and work occupying a place in the whole. This was the American heritage, the Great American Novel.

At that point, having transcribed 80 years of canonical fiction, we could no longer regard the works he put on the syllabus as a casual matter of the teacher’s taste. For the next nine months, we’d be served a slice of an exclusive tradition, some of the best but not all. It made each novel more important. The plights of Henry Fleming, Frederic Henry, and Quentin Compson were personal to me, it turned out, and to believe that they marked special moments in American literary history enhanced my identification. Reading each work became a noble and fateful endeavor.

The courses presented a tiny model of or outlook upon time and being. They told me that the past contains momentous objects that fall into a plot. The implication was inescapable in courses that assigned materials from long ago that laid claim to greatness and influence.

I believe that such conclusions are drawn by students all the time. Whether a teacher intends it or not, the syllabus in any course with a historical or aesthetic dimension implies a picture of reality.

In my 11th Grade class, with a canon of masterful writings in hand, I learned that there is significance in the course of human events, that a record of achievement is waiting to be learned. Another syllabus, one without chronological order and that mixed pop culture with classics, might have led me to the opposite beliefs.

What a contrast that outlook is to the experience pressed upon the 15-year-old of today by media of all kinds, social and entertainment. What comes through the small and large screen amounts to a swarm of images, chatter, music, voices, videos, photos, sports highlights, celebrity profiles, games, and youth news. It’s a blooming, buzzing confusion that has no depth, no history, no rational sequence. A youth flooded with media easily assumes that existence itself is equally unstable and unstructured and indifferent to quality.

A humanistic course that puts superb materials into a coherent narrative with purpose and momentum can curb the unease. When teachers craft their syllabi, they should ask, “What am I implying about the universe? What am I saying about the past? Am I handing them a world that they shall be eager to join?” The implicit outlook of a course that puts the greats into a grand narrative can be a worthy antidote to the chaos that engulfs them the moment they leave the school grounds.
